items.title: Timber grid and external stair offer "a wink" to Centre Pompidou at its annexe in Massy
items.summary:
French architecture studio PCA-Stream has completed Centre Pompidou Francilien in Massy, a storage and exhibition space fronted by a gridded timber deck and external stair that echo the high-tech character of the iconic original Centre Pompidou in Paris.

Officially named Centre Pompidou Francilien Fabrique de l'Art (Art Factory), the 30,000-square-metre building is the first Centre Pompidou annexe in Île-de-France. It is scheduled to open to the public in spring 2027.

Photographs 

Previous 

Next 

Photographs

Close 

Overlooking a small lake, the building will house over 150,000 pieces from the Centre Pompidou's reserve collections made visible to the public through temporary exhibition spaces, alongside private conservation and restoration areas.

It was built around a nine-metre cubic grid described by the studio as "a giant Sol LeWitt " artwork, which creates open, flexible spaces for both storage and exhibitions.

The grid is fronted by an open timber frame and traversed via an external staircase dubbed "the caterpillar", nodding to the glass-tube escalators at the original Pompidou Centre in Beaubourg, Paris.

"The brief posed a paradoxical question: how do you display what normally remains invisible?" PCA-Stream founder Philippe Chiambretta told Dezeen.

"What truly constitutes the spirit of Beaubourg is not its image but its principle: large, flexible floor plates, made possible by great constructive rationality, which leave the institution free to reinvent its uses over time. That is the heritage we wanted to carry into Massy," he added.

items.title: A Former Appliance Store Becomes a Hong Kong Cocktail Bar
items.summary:
Good design is all about transformation and turning the everyday into memorable spaces. Kevin Yiu, principal at Minus Workshop , did just that with his recent conversion of a former appliance store into Mius , a cocktail bar in Hong Kong.

Nestled at 29 Gough Street in the SoHo district, the space reflects owner Shelley Tai’s belief in simple things done right, from libations that honor the classics to comfort food without complication. “Her desire for a genuine neighborhood bar challenged me to translate that specific vibe into spatial design,” Yiu explains.

Photography by Steven Ko

Yiu embraced mid-century modern design, and with only eight months to complete the project, he turned constraints into assets. High ceilings and a curated system of leather blinds capture sunlight by day, then offer layered illumination in the evening. A low structural beam clad in oak now doubles as an element that guides circulation and visually organizes the spaces. Electrical and mechanical systems remain hidden by joinery, which still allows access for maintenance.

Photography by Steven Ko

The material palette blends a range of contrasting textures. Wood veneer adds an organic appeal, while bronze and silver metals cast a subtle sheen, paired with shades of copper and brown. Minimal paint, rather than the artificial brightness of lacquer, keeps the aesthetic grounded.

Photography by Steven Ko

The 14-foot stainless steel bar top is both a statement piece and a functional surface that integrates essential equipment for the staff. Slabs of travertine form high tables where guests enjoy…
items.t: A Former Appliance Store Becomes a Hong Kong Cocktail Bar

items.title: Programa extension brings SketchUp models and product schedules into one workflow
items.summary:
Studio operations software Programa has introduced a SketchUp extension that connects 3D models with its product Schedules, freeing designers from duplicating information and giving them more creative time.

According to Programa, the extension is designed to reduce duplicate data entry by connecting a 3D model in SketchUp with a project’s Schedule in Programa.

Programa’s Schedule s function acts as a streamlined alternative to spreadsheets, detailing each item’s code, supplier, finish, dimensions, quantity and price.

Programa helps architects and designers manage their projects 

The extension runs inside SketchUp and allows designers to link components in the model to matching products in the Schedule.

As a result, designers can track an item from the first 3D sketch through to its final specification, without entering the same information separately in SketchUp and Programa.

From the model, designers can send a component to a chosen Schedule, or link it to a product that is already listed there.

Programa explained that linking to an existing product creates a connection without adding a duplicate line item, keeping the Schedule "clean" as the design is fleshed out.

Before anything is added, designers can review and edit the product’s information.

The Schedule entry combines the details available from the component with anything entered during that review.

Programa said this gives studios a chance to check the specification before it is used for pricing or procurement.

The extension also provides access to Programa’s Product Library within SketchUp.

items.t: Programa extension brings SketchUp models and product schedules into one workflow

items.title: Estúdio 41 wraps coastal Brazilian house in white brise-soleil
items.summary:
Brazilian firm Estúdio 41 has completed Guaratuba House, which features exterior screens and a structural system that "explores the architectural expression of exposed precast concrete ".

Located in the seaside community of Prainha, which sits within the city of Guaratuba in southern Brazil, the holiday home was designed for a family to serve as "a refuge between the mountains and the sea". 

"One of their main requirements was, therefore, a strong visual connection between the interior spaces and the surrounding natural landscape," said Estúdio 41 , an architectural firm based in Curitiba.

Drawings and photographs 

Previous 

Next 

Drawings and photographs

Close 

Ground floor plan

First floor plan

Rectangular in plan, the 375-square-metre house has two floors. It is wrapped in folding screens made of perforated melamine panels.

The screens filter natural light and reduce solar gain on glass surfaces. When opened up, they reveal views of the scenic landscape.

"At night, the transparency and geometric patterns of the house's skin give it the appearance of a lantern within the landscape," the team said.

To protect against flooding, as the coastal site has been affected by storm surges in the past, the building was lifted up 70 centimeters (2.3 feet).

It has a prefabricated concrete structural system that was assembled in only six hours, with the concrete structural elements left visible.

items.title: Friday Five with Nick Doyle: Seeing America Through Shades of Blue
items.summary:
Creative minds can seemingly turn anything into art—from household items and food to packing supplies and bottle caps. For Los Angeles-born interdisciplinary artist Nick Doyle , the material of choice is denim. Even when working in other mediums, he often gravitates toward a denim-blue palette, as in his latest exhibition, “ Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found .”

Presented at Pace Prints ’ New York gallery this fall, the exhibition marks Doyle’s first venture into printmaking, using graphic interpretations of everyday objects to examine American preoccupations with risk and reward, escapism, and the myth of the self-made man. The gallery will present a selection of these works at Art Basel Miami Beach 2026 .

‘Quick Fix’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

Now based in Brooklyn, Doyle earned a BFA in interdisciplinary arts from the San Francisco Art Institute and an MFA in sculpture from Hunter College, in addition to studying at Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture . He cites his discovery of denim as an artistic medium as a turning point in his career.

“I had been doing a ton of research on American history and making work exploring our relationship to nostalgia,” he recalls. “One day a fashion designer moved out of the neighboring studio and threw away a ton of stuff. I found a bolt of denim, and my brain flashed across a network of ideas I had already been considering. I intuitively knew I had stumbled across something significant.”

Photography courtesy of Pace Prints

items.title: Meet Kiki Goti, Kelly Wearstler's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
items.summary:
Next up in Dezeen's 20x20 project in partnership with  Kohler , which marks 20 years of Dezeen, is Greek designer Kiki Goti, who was nominated by Kelly Wearstler for her innovative approach to ornament and artisanship.

Goti has experienced a remarkable rise since presenting a furniture collection made from salvaged foam insulation during the 2023 edition of Milan design week .

Her conceptual, research-led work typically explores heritage, identity and craftsmanship, resulting in playful objects and spaces that reexamine the cultural codes embedded in design.

Goti was nominated as an emerging talent to watch by American designer Wearstler , who praised how Goti “approaches ornament with the precision of an engineer and the instincts of a sculptor”.

“That refusal to treat craft and technology as opposites is going to matter more over the next 20 years,” Wearstler added.

Kelly Wearstler (above) has picked Kiki Goti (right) for Dezeen's 20x20 project. Photo courtesy of H&M Home 

Goti recently relocated from New York to Paris. Photo by Liz Carababas 

As well as a shared love of ornament and the decorative arts, Wearstler also picked up on how Goti's practice is informed by her background in robotics and machine learning.

“It's amazing to be nominated by such a big designer, and also someone who shares my passion for craft and attention to detail,” Goti told Dezeen.

items.title: Hawkins\Brown's temporary housing for homeless families in London is a UK first
items.summary:
Architecture studio Hawkins\Brown has unveiled the Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre in London , the first purpose-built development to provide temporary accommodation for homeless families in the UK .

Situated in the London Borough of Havering, the centre contains 74 flats for families and two floors of community space built around a central courtyard.

Plans and exterior photographs 

Previous 

Next 

Plans and exterior photographs

Close 

Ground floor plan

Typical upper floor plan

Forming part of the wider regeneration of Harold Hill Estate, Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre was designed to help alleviate the growing demand for temporary housing in the local borough.

Intending to set a benchmark for temporary family housing in the UK, Hawkins\Brown aimed to create a welcoming building that eases the stress of families facing homelessness.

"Many of the families who come here are fleeing hugely painful domestic situations," said Hawkins\Brown partner Nick Gaskell. 

"The Harold Hill Family Welcome Centre aims to make a traumatic period a little more bearable by providing a caring, calming and uplifting environment for as long as they need it."

Designed to be in keeping with the neighbouring buildings, the exterior of the U-shaped building is lined with striped bands of orange-toned bricks and pops of pale green metal sheeting.

A secure, landscaped courtyard with play space at the centre of the building helps bring natural light into the surrounding flats.

items.title: Rachel Whiteread punctures 2027 Brit Award trophy
items.summary:
Artist Rachel Whiteread has revealed her design for next year's Brit Awards trophy, a silver sculpture covered in holes to "expose the interior of the statue".

Since 1992, a different creative has been selected to design the handheld trophy for the UK music industry's annual Brit Awards .

Essex-born Whiteread has designed the statuette for next February's ceremony, which is her interpretation of the annual trophy depicting Britannia, a helmeted warrior that is a traditional symbol of Britain.

The result is a minimalist silver statuette cast in resin and covered in holes to draw attention to the inside of the trophy.

"I exposed the interior of the statue, as an artist would do with their music," said Whiteread.

Whiteread then handpainted the nickel-plated trophy in a silver hue.

The artist is known for casting everyday architectural forms, such as staircases or sheds , in materials including plaster and concrete to showcase their negative space.

Read:

Yinka Ilori reveals Tottenham Hotspur away shirt 

She explained that when designing the Brit Award, she wanted to put her own spin on the recognisable trophy.

"I saw this as a natural extension of my work – to continue to celebrate and recognise British art and creativity," said Whiteread.

"Art and culture are under very real threat," she continued. "So I was grateful to be able to take a tangible role in highlighting the importance of safeguarding creativity through the design of this year's trophy and standing together as artists, whether from music or the visual arts."

The Brit Awards will take place on 27…
items.t: Rachel Whiteread punctures 2027 Brit Award trophy

items.title: "We wanted to avoid the idea of tropical modernism" says curator of Geoffrey Bawa exhibition at Vitra Design Museum
items.summary:
As the Vitra Design Museum hosts Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses, the first major retrospective of the Sri Lankan architect in over 20 years, co-curator Johan Deurell explains why the 'tropical modernist' label has confused Bawa's legacy.

Geoffrey Bawa is one of Asia's most prolific 20th-century architects, known for projects such as the Bentota Beach Hotel, the Kandalama Hotel and his own houses, Number 11 and Lunuganga.

Bawa's work is often described as tropical modernist, as it is seen to blend Western modernist principles with Sri Lankan vernacular traditions and materials.

But Deurell said he and his co-curators deliberately stayed away from this label, which was coined by Western architects and scholars and is closely associated with British colonialism.

Bawa's designs include his house in Colombo, Number 11 (also above) 

Geoffrey Bawa is pictured here with one of his four dogs, circa 1989 

"We wanted to avoid the idea of tropical modernism," he told Dezeen.

"It comes with so much baggage. But it's also not the most useful tool to discuss Geoffrey Bawa's work with."

As one of the Vitra Design Museum's in-house curators, Deurell oversaw the show with Shayari de Silva, chief curator for the Geoffrey Bawa Trust , and Ikko Yokoyama, a senior curator at M+ in Hong Kong.

The exhibition offers a broader understanding of Bawa's legacy, highlighting qualities that set him apart from the modernists.

For instance, it highlights how his buildings worked with existing landscape conditions.

items.t: "We wanted to avoid the idea of tropical modernism" says curator of Geoffrey Bawa exhibition at Vitra Design Museum

items.title: "How did young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?"
items.summary:
In the face of planetary collapse, design education and practice need to change to show young designers that it's possible for them to make a difference, writes Céline Semaan .

The last time I taught a design class, at the School of Visual Arts (SVA) in New York, I remember sitting in my car after the two-hour workshop feeling quite honestly distraught. How had these young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?

During class, we discussed the political, ecological and economic infrastructures that make design possible: mineral extraction, exploited labour and the colonial systems sustaining much of what we produce and consume. 

Having assumed these conversations had become an expected part of design education, I was taken aback by how little the students cared. Instead, they were far more concerned with securing and keeping jobs in an increasingly precarious industry.

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience

“How do you expect us to make any difference if this is how the industry works?” one asked. Another just wanted to know how to earn a living, without upsetting their employers. 

These were excellent questions, particularly as designers now compete with artificial intelligence capable of executing instructions at extraordinary speed. If design is reduced to following briefs and producing outputs, what space is there for a designer to effect any structural change?

Perhaps the profession needs to reconsider its relationship with obedience. Designers are trained to solve problems, yet rarely encouraged to question…
items.t: "How did young designers become so convinced of their own powerlessness?"

items.title: Burlwood Is Making a Comeback With a Modern Twist
items.summary:
Few materials make a visual statement quite like burlwood. Its swirls and naturally irregular patterns give it a depth and individuality that are difficult to replicate. That distinctive grain comes from burls, rounded growths that develop on tree trunks or branches and are often associated with injury, stress, or infection.

Burlwood gained popularity during the Art Deco era of the 1920s and ’30s before becoming a defining feature of furniture design in the 1970s. Today, it’s experiencing another moment. Yet its current appeal is less about recreating the past and more about rethinking how the material fits modern spaces.

Design Milk spoke with four designers to learn why burlwood continues to resonate and the fresh ways they’re using it.

Bookmatched burlwood creates a striking symmetrical pattern across this three-drawer chest, set against a sculptural curved wood bed frame. Photography by Emily Hart.

Why Burlwood Continues to Captivate Designers 
 “Burlwood does what a great print does,” says Tiffany Brooks , principal designer of Tiffany Brooks Interiors . “It gives your eye somewhere to go. Up close, you see all these little swirls and knots, and from across the room, it reads as one rich surface. Even two pieces made from the same wood can have completely different personalities.”

Abbe Fenimore , owner of Studio Ten 25 , shares that appreciation for burlwood’s organic qualities, seeing the material as a way to introduce visual interest without relying on patterned textiles.

The tightly patterned grain of this burlwood chest extends across its drawer fronts,…

“Scandinavian design never shouts, but when you come closer, you are rewarded,” says Sara Erichsen Susnjar, senior color and material design manager at Volvo Cars . Detail by detail, the automaker’s new all-electric EX60 bears this out. Its seats carry a pattern drawn from two seas converging off the coast of Skagen, Denmark; its base carpet borrows its hue from foraged finds from the woods outside the company’s studio in Sweden; and an interior lighting option fills the cabin with the silhouettes of leaves.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars

Erichsen Susnjar, who has spent 20 years at Volvo Cars, oversaw color and materials for both the EX60 and the EX60 Cross Country. Under her direction, the team looked to the natural world for the car’s colors, patterns, and textures, often starting with what turned up on a walk.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars

Forest Finds 
 Gathering began close to home, on outings that were already part of the team’s routine. “We are very fortunate to have the forest just outside our design studio, so it naturally becomes part of our everyday life, whether we go there for lunch, a coffee break, or simply to clear our minds,” Erichsen Susnjar says.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars

Over time, the team began bringing small pieces of the landscape back inside: mushrooms, twigs, stones, moss, and herbs. items.title: The Best Gifts for Cooks, Chefs, and the Culinary Curious
items.summary:
The holiday season brings plenty of opportunities to gather around the table, and for those who love to cook, eat, and experiment in the kitchen, there’s no shortage of gift possibilities. A good gift should feel personal, whether it’s an object they’ll use for years or an ingredient worth sharing around the table.

This year’s selections come with stories of their own. There’s a Oaxacan potter who grows copal and tobacco to finish his clay, a Norwegian fisherman’s daughter who became convinced seaweed is the food of the future, and a former line cook who declared she had an apron company before she actually did.

You’ll find serving pieces that make entertaining easier, ingredients that start conversations, and small but indispensable kitchen tools that prove thoughtful doesn’t have to mean extravagant. Some are made for the table, others for the kitchen, and a few might inspire an entirely new culinary adventure.

After all, the best gifts give everyone something to enjoy, whether it’s a new flavor to try or a good story to share.

items.title: ‘The Terence Conran of his day’: the visionary Victorian futurist adored by design superstars today
items.summary:
A professor at the age of 21, Christopher Dresser was a design genius who created beautiful, futuristic homeware, from teapots to toast racks to jugs. Why is his brilliance only now being recognised?

Victorian industrial designer Christopher Dresser was always a visionary. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. He became a professor at 21, dreaming up theories based on plant structure that changed the way designers worked.

But it was after he quit academia that he really started to break boundaries. As a self-declared “design doctor”, he experimented with production techniques that brought beautiful, futuristic homeware into everyday houses. He was one of the first western designers to travel to Japan, helping introduce Japonisme to British life, which has had a transformative effect on furniture and decoration ever since.

items.title: Davis Furniture and jehs+laub Introduce the Sculptural Laken Nesting Tables
items.summary:
Three steel parts shape the silhouette of the Laken Occasional Table Series : a spun cone settling low against the floor, a slender column drawing upward from its center, and a second cone opening wide to cradle a circular top. The dual-cone composition gives jehs+laub ’s design for Davis Furniture its distinctly modern profile, extended to a set of three nesting tables.

Designed to nest seamlessly or stand alone, the three round tables scale from a single grouping to individual pieces. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Laken continues a collaboration between Davis and jehs+laub that began in 2009, and it carries forward the studio’s approach to balancing soft curvature with precise, architectural form. On every Laken table, gentle radii and careful proportions ease the move from flared base to slender column to inverted cone, and each piece appears fully resolved from any angle.

Nested together or used on their own, the tables can be layered into a single, dynamic arrangement or spread throughout an interior, adapting to lounge, hospitality, and collaborative environments.

Each round tabletop is supported by an inverted steel cone. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

The sculptural form belies a carefully engineered base. Its spun steel cones and steel column are mechanically fastened through concealed hardware for a tight, durable assembly built to perform over time, and a ballast hidden within the lower cone brings the center of gravity down, giving the tables stability and resistance to tipping.

items.title: ‘An extravagantly illuminated beast’: the best artificial Christmas trees in the UK – tested
items.summary:
Pick wisely, and your fake fir could be reused for decades of Decembers. From pre-lit to frosted to space-saving, here are our festive favourites

• The best beauty Advent calendars
• The best Christmas baubles

In the 70s and 80s Essex of my youth, no one had a real Christmas tree unless they lived in the country, or perhaps Loughton. Our family’s skinny artificial tree is now 55 years old and comes out every year at my sister’s. It’s shed a few plastic “needles” down the years, but it’s still standing proud – which is more than you can say for a real Christmas tree bought in 1971, or even 2025.

Therein lies the surprising environmental efficiency of artificial Christmas trees. The Carbon Trust says using a fake tree over seven to 20 years (depending on its weight and materials) can create fewer emissions than buying a new, commercially grown tree every year. The key is to buy an artificial tree you’ll love enough to roll out for decades.

items.title: Fireclay Tile Turns Traditional Textiles Into Hand-Painted Tile
items.summary:
Plaids and florals might seem more at home on upholstery or wallpaper than ceramic tile, but Fireclay Tile’s latest collection makes a compelling case for bringing those familiar patterns to harder surfaces. Called Idyllwild, the new hand-painted collection takes inspiration from traditional textiles, translating everything from delicate botanical illustrations to richly layered plaids into ceramic designs that feel both nostalgic and contemporary.

Interestingly, the collection didn’t begin with flowers at all. “We were seeing designers use a lot of intricate textiles, colors, and patterns together,” explains Jamie Chappell, VP of Brand and Product at Fireclay Tile, adding that early explorations focused on plaids and stripes. “As a true lover of ’90s alt-rock, I actually went down a rabbit hole early on, wondering if it should be a ‘grunge’ collection.”

Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection in its Winter palette, featuring deep blues, earthy greens, and warm neutrals across floral, striped, and plaid patterns.

That direction eventually gave way to something softer. Recognizing the longstanding relationship between florals and plaids in interiors, the team introduced botanical patterns to balance the collection’s more structured designs. The name Idyllwild followed, referencing the California mountain town.

The resulting collection includes 16 patterns organized into four categories: Specimen Flowers, Idyllwild Florals, Idyllwild Stripes, and Idyllwild Plaids.

The Specimen Flowers series features four individual botanical motifs—Allium, Carnation, Lily, and…

items.title: Art Meets the Slopes at Powder Mountain’s Outdoor Gallery
items.summary:
Most skiers and snowboarders will likely pause at some point during a day on the slopes to take in their surroundings. After all, ski resorts typically offer great mountain views. But at Powder Mountain in Utah, visitors get more than a scenic view. They might also encounter a bright pink pineapple rising among the pines, a classical Greek column twisted into an improbable shape, or poetry carved into a boulder. These three installations are the latest additions to Powder Art Foundation ’s skiable outdoor art museum, an evolving collection that challenges how—and where—we experience art.

Davina Semo’s Listener (2020–2024), a patinated cast-bronze bell, is part of Powder Art Foundation’s outdoor art collection at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography courtesy of Powder Art Foundation.

Established in 2024 in partnership with Dia Art Foundation , Powder Art Foundation occupies 8,000 acres of Utah’s Wasatch Mountains. The foundation’s goal is to bring contemporary installations into dialogue with the landscape while honoring the region’s connection to the Land Art movement.

“We’re building a collection that people encounter while spending time outdoors, so I’m interested in work that can surprise you and hold your attention without needing a museum around it,” says Alex Zhang, chief creative officer of Powder Mountain.
